Book Discussion | Book Launch -- Absence/Presence: 30 Years of Day Without Art


The afternoon will bring together former Visual AIDS staff and contributors to the book for a series of short conversations spanning the history of Day Without Art. Editors Kyle Croft and Risa Puleo will reflect on the project’s emergence and its first decade; Amy Sadao and Nelson Santos will discuss its evolution through the 2000s; and Ted Kerr and Elizabeth Koke will consider Day Without Art from the 2010s to the present. Together, the conversations will reflect on the people who sustained the project, and how its strategies have changed alongside the AIDS epidem

Book Discussion | Magic Historian Shares Her Memoir about the "Queen of Magic" (In Person AND Online!)


The multi-media presentation will include an illustrated talk, magic performances, and a display of rarely seen Madame Adelaide Herrmann memorabilia, followed by a book signing. In her day, Madame Adelaide Herrmann was more famous than her younger colleague, Harry Houdini. For nearly sixty years, Adelaide Herrmann (1853-1932) ruled the global stage. She caught speeding bullets with her bare hands. She soared through the air as a human cannonball. Alongside her husband, Alexander, she executed the most mesmerizing illusions of the Golden Age of Magic. Then tragedy struck. Widowed at forty-three, Adelaide stepped into the magician's role as the sole headliner. For three thrilling decades, she reigned supreme as vaudeville's Queen of Magic. Copies of Queen of Magic: The Wondrous, Unstoppable Adelaide Herrmann will be available for purchase at the event.
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Book Discussion | Streetscape Photographers Discuss Their Book Blending New York History, Culinary Culture, & Interior Design


Photographers James T. and Karla L. Murray speak about their most recent book, Counter Culture, and some of our neighborhoods' and New York's most iconic lunch spots such as B&H Dairy and Veselka. For more than a century, New York City's Mom & Pop diners and luncheonettes have been serving the melting pot, piping fresh and hot. Under the warm glow of neon lights, local landmarks like the Lexington Candy Shop and La Bonbonniere offer an escape from the frenetic pace of daily life, while others like Tom's Restaurant are elevated to pop culture fame, appearing as an exterior locale on Seinfeld and inspiring Suzanne Vega's folk song turned club classic, "Tom's Diner." Blending New York history, culinary culture, and interior design with epicurean delight, Counter Culture offers a wealth of details to be savored at length over a black-and-white cookie. Perch on a swivel stool along the sweeping Formica counter where the action is hot, or slide into a cozy booth, perusing the sumptuous array of comfort foods like syrup-soaked pancakes, classic burger and fries, and bottomless mugs of coffee -- or sample family favorites from the old country, like Greek gyros, Ukrainian borscht, Cuban sandwiches, Thai disco fries, and Korean fried chicken wings. In Counter Culture, there's a little something for everyone.
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Talk | MIT Museum Professional Shares Interactive Projects Currently in the Works


What if a museum worked less like a warehouse for finished objects and more like a lab where the experiment is still running? Ann Neumann is the Director of Galleries and Exhibitions at MIT Museum, and led its 2022 move into a new 56,000-square-foot space in Kendall Square. Ann will walk the group through the multiple interactive projects she's shepherded at the MIT Museum. These projects work as prototypes for engaging the public with technologies like CRISPR, machine learning, and sensory neuroscience. Through it all, she asks: can a museum work as infrastructure for public experimentation, rather than simply a room we walk through? Ann is a strategic museum leader, designer, and curator. She’s the recipient of numerous awards for her work and was named a Lollop Museum Influencer in 2024. 
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Discussion | Live Conversation with Winners of 2026 Humanities Prizes


Each year the American Council of Learned Societies recognizes and rewards the authors and publishers of exceptional, innovative, and open humanities scholarship. Open access publishing offers exciting new opportunities for scholars to share their research with wider audiences. This event will feature a live conversation with winners of the 2026 prizes, which are awarded in the categories of Anthropology, Environmental Humanities, History, Literary/Media Studies, Multimodal, and Political Science. Conversations will be moderated by Beth Daley, Executive Editor of the nonprofit news website The Conversation. This year’s winners are: Anthropology  | Mal-Nutrition: Maternal Health Science and the Reproduction of Harm by Emily Yates-Doerr (University of California Press, 2024) Environmental Humanities | Ecological States: Politics of Science and Nature in Urbanizing China by Jesse Rodenbiker (Cornell University Press, 2023) History | Abortion Pills: US History and Politics by Carrie Baker (Amherst College Press, 2024) Literary/Media Studies | Twining: Critical and Creative Approaches to Hypertext Narratives by Anastasia Salter and Stuart Moulthrop (Amherst College Press, 2021) Multimodal | Deaf Mobility Studies: Exploring International Networks, Tourism, and Migration by Annelies Kusters, Erin Moriarty, Amandine le Maire, Sanchayeeta Iyer, and Steven Emery (Gallaudet University Press, 2024) Political Science | Renegotiating Patriarchy: Gender, Agency, and the Bangladesh Paradox by Naila Kabeer (LSE Press, 2024)

Book Discussion | Journalists Share Their Books on Boundary-Breaking Art & the Ongoing Fight To Defend Creative Freedom


Martha Wilson and Anne Turyn present two groundbreaking publications documenting 1970s-1980s New York Avant-Garde performance and bookmaking. Artist and Franklin Furnace founder Martha Wilson will discuss her new book, Back to the Present: 50 Years of Free Expression with Franklin Furnace, a 50th-anniversary celebration of the legendary arts institution Franklin Furnace. This visually rich volume captures five decades of boundary-breaking art and the ongoing fight to defend creative freedom. Further, it chronicles stories by individuals from arts groups across the U.S.A. who also fought in the Culture Wars of the Reagan 80s. Anne Turyn, a New York-based fine art photographer, will share Top Stories, a prose periodical that she edited and published from 1978 to 1991. Over the course of twenty-nine issues, it served as a pivotal platform for experimental fiction and art through single-artist issues and two anthologies. Primarily featuring female artists, though in Turyn’s words a few men “crept in as collaborators."

Lecture | Princeton Archeologist Discusses the Traveling Craftsmen of Ancient Greece


The designs of Greek temples, with their recognizable Doric and Ionic columns, spread widely in the ancient Mediterranean and Black Sea in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. The dissemination of these architectural forms depended on highly mobile stone masons, who cross-pollinated design ideas as they worked far from home. Sam Holzman- Assistant Professor of Art & Archaeology at Princeton University- presents a talk that surveys a range of evidence for the mobility of ancient builders, from inscribed records to new lead-isotope analysis.
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Conference | Artists & Scholars Revisit the Legacy of the 1956 Congress of Black Writers and Artists (In Person AND Online!)


In 1956, the First Congress of Black Writers and Artists took place in Paris. It inaugurated the "postcolonial moment" in Europe and Africa, quickly followed by a lesser-known second one, in 1959 in Rome. To celebrate this 70th anniversary, attendees ask: what would a congress be today? Namely, how did the 1950's stakes evolved? which territorities, minorities and discourses have been left apart? what can these two Congresses teach us today and what can we add to them? Speakers/Artists: Nelson Maldonado-Torres is a Professor of Philosophy at the University of Connecticut and a leading voice in decolonial theory. Nadia Yala Kisukidi is an Associate Professor at the NYU Department of French Literature, Thought, and Culture. Grégory Pierrot is an Associate Professor of English at the University of Connecticut, Stamford, specializing in the cultural networks of the Black Atlantic. Mame-Fatou Niang is a Professor of French & Francophone Studies and founder of the Center for Black European Studies and the Atlantic at Carnegie Mellon University. A scholar, filmmaker, and photographer, she co-directed the documentary Mariannes Noires and authored Identités françaises and Universalisme. Junior Mintt is a Brooklyn-based drag artist, comedian, and Black trans activist, host of The Junior Mintt Show, an independent late-night program centered on Blackness, queerness, and radical positivity. Brent Hayes Edwards is a Peng Family Professor of English and Comparative Literature at Columbia University, affiliated with its Center for Jazz Studies. He is the author of The Practice of Diaspora, winner of the John Hope Franklin Prize, and Epistrophies: Jazz and the Literary Imagination. Mistura Allison is an independent researcher, curator, and art historian based between London and Milan, currently Curator and Project Coordinator at Villa Romana in Florence. She is the founder of ashikọ, a research platform centered on contemporary diasporic visual and oral production from Africa and its diaspora. Seumboy Vrainom is a French artist, writer, and self-described "digital shaman apprentice" whose work critiques colonial history through appropriated internet imagery and DIY video. An advocate for decolonial ecology, he is a contributor to the media outlet Histoires Crépues.
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Discussion | Clinical Psychologist Discusses Seasonal Affective Disorder & Management Strategies


A discussion with William Lamson, Ph.D. including common symptoms, factors that may contribute to seasonal changes in mood, and strategies for managing symptoms and supporting mental and emotional wellbeing during the winter months. Seasonal Affective Disorder is a type of depression that occurs at certain times of the year, most commonly during the fall and winter months. Changes in daylight and seasonal routines may affect mood, sleep, energy, and daily functioning. Understanding the signs and symptoms of Seasonal Affective Disorder, as well as available treatment and management strategies, can help individuals recognize when seasonal changes may be affecting their wellbeing and identify approaches to support their mental health.

Book Discussion | Pulitzer Prize–Winning Journalist Shares Her New Book, Safe Passage


Evelyn Iritani uncovers the little-known story of the dangerous negotiations that led to the exchange of American and Japanese civilians during World War II. In the fall of 1943, as some of the Second World War’s bloodiest battles unfolded across the Pacific, the United States and Japan pulled off a diplomatic coup—the return of civilians caught on the wrong side of the battlefield after Pearl Harbor. In Safe Passage, journalist Evelyn Iritani reveals the rarely told story behind this wartime exchange, featuring a cast of determined diplomats, sharp-tongued journalists, missionaries, and refugees—and the difficult choices involved in bringing everyone home. Iritani sheds new light on this remarkable story of diplomacy and survival.

Book Discussion | Ecologist Shares His New Book, Before New York (In Person AND Online!)


Eric Sanderson in conversation with Michael Kimmelman.  In Before New York, Eric W. Sanderson invites readers on a breathtaking journey through the evolution of New York City—its natural features, inhabitants, and geography—from long before Henry Hudson's arrival in 1609 up to the present day. This monumental work is the culmination of more than 25 years of research, featuring 75 original maps, 200 color illustrations, and nearly 4,000 detailed descriptions of streams, wetlands, rocks, plants, animals, and Indigenous settlements. An epic expansion of Sanderson's bestselling and critically acclaimed book Mannahatta, this atlas and gazetteer brings to life the lost world of Welikia, land we now describe as the five boroughs of New York City, revealing what has vanished, what survives, and what could be restored with vision and care.

Gallery Talk | Art History Talk: Discover the Life & legacy of Joan Miro


Explore the life and work of an iconic modern artist. Miró’s works are hard to classify but do express his pride in his Catalan heritage (references to Barcelona and the countryside) and his contempt for conventional art. The unconscious and subconscious interact with a child-like wonder and dreamlike imagery so he might be dubbed a surrealist. After 1920, he spent winters in Paris and summers on the family farm near Barcelona. He directly influenced Pollock, Calder, and Rothko. His themes are sex, humor, nature, excrement, and playfulness along with fear and anger. He worked in oil, gouache, bronze, and ceramics.

Book Club | Novella Discussion: Recent Novel by Award-Winning Author


At this book club session, the group will discuss Olga Ravn's 2025 book, The Wax Child, translated from Danish by Martin Aitken. In seventeenth-century Denmark, Christenze Kruckow, an unmarried noblewoman, is accused of witchcraft. She and several other women are rumored to be possessed by the Devil, who has come to them in the form of a tall headless man and gives them dark powers: they can steal people's happiness, they have performed unchristian acts, and they can cause pestilence or even death. They are all in danger of the stake. The Wax Child, narrated by a wax doll created by Christenze Kruckow, is an unsettling horror story about brutality and power, nature and witchcraft, set in the fragile communities of premodern Europe.  Deeply researched and steeped in visceral, atmospheric detail, The Wax Child is based on a series of real witchcraft trials that took place in Northern Jutland in the seventeenth century. Full of lush storytelling and alarmingly rich imagination, Olga Ravn weaves in quotes from original sources such as letters, magical spells and manuals, court documents, and Scandinavian grimoires.

Book Discussion | A Postwar German Literary Masterpiece Rediscovered: Translator & Novelest Discuss


Illusions' translator Rob Madole joins writer Megan Nolan for a conversation about this book. Upon publication, critics were baffled by author Ruth Rehmann's frank treatment of sexuality—mistaking it for frivolousness—and faulted her style for “an excess of contemporaneity.” Read today, its focus on the poverty of human connection within an abundant and stubbornly traditional society feels shockingly prescient. Illusions follows four employees of the Wellis Corporation over one unsatisfactory weekend: grey-haired secretary Frau Schramm, frustrated translator Paul Westermann, fadingly glamorous Carmen Viol, and restless young assistant Therese Pfeiffer. Narrated in a prismatic, stream-of-consciousness style that jumps fluidly among characters, the book offers a portrait of the claustrophobic tension beneath postwar capitalism. Originally published by Suhrkamp in 1959 during West Germany's "economic miracle," Illusions incisively examines a regime attempting to slough off its Nazi past through a zealous drive to modernize and a rhetoric of material abundance.
   Manhattan, New York, NY

Discussion | Johns Hopkins Bioethics Researchers Discuss Advances in Reproductive Technology


Speakers explore the promises, risks, and societal implications of a technology that could reshape the future of human reproduction. What if ordinary skin cells could be transformed into eggs or sperm? Scientists are exploring in vitro gametogenesis (IVG), a technology that could expand reproductive options while raising profound ethical questions.  Jeffrey Kahn, PhD, MPH is the Andreas C. Dracopoulos Director of the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics and the Levi Professor of Bioethics and Public Policy. His work focuses on the ethics of research, ethics and public health including global health, and ethics and emerging biomedical technologies. He speaks widely in the US and abroad, has published five books and over 160 articles, and is a member of the National Academy of Medicine. Anna Mastroianni, JD, MPH, is Research Professor in Bioethics and Law at the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics. Her scholarship explores complex issues at the intersection of law, bioethics, public health, and health policy, with a particular focus on the challenges of research in pregnancy, genetic technologies, and family building through assisted reproductive technologies. She has published widely across these areas and is recognized for her contributions to major debates in bioethics and public policy.

About the book: Abruptly deceased at the age of twenty-four and trapped forever in flared purple trousers, Liwa Ekimakingaï encounters the other residents of Frère Lachaise cemetery, all of whom have their own complex stories of life and death.  Unwilling to relinquish their tender bond, Liwa makes his way back home to Pointe-Noire to see his devoted grandmother one last time, against all spectral advice.
